summary: Specifies an optional Content-MD5 header field for MIME messages that carries a digest of the content, so a receiver can check that the message was not corrupted. It is a draft standard.

eli5.summary: A fingerprint attached to a message so the receiver can tell if anything got damaged.

questions: how to check mime message integrity
subtitle: An optional MIME header that carries an MD5 digest so a receiver can check a message body arrived intact.

tldr.problem: Even with MIME's protections, it is useful to be able to verify that the decoded data of a message are the same data that were originally sent.
tldr.mechanism: The originating mail program computes the MD5 digest of the canonical form of the content, base64-encodes the 16 bytes, and puts the result in a Content-MD5 header field.
tldr.outcome: It protects against accidental modification only, not deliberate tampering. RFC 1864 obsoletes RFC 1544.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 1864 as a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 1544. No RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: A Message Integrity Check
sections.content:
MIME tries to protect data during email transport, but it is still desirable to verify that the data, once decoded, are intact. This memo defines the optional Content-MD5 header field as a message integrity check. It may also appear in the encapsulated headers of a message/external-body object to verify the retrieved data.

MD5 computes a 128 bit digest of arbitrary-length data with a high degree of confidence that any change in the data changes the digest. The algorithm is defined elsewhere (RFC 1321); this memo specifies how to use it for MIME mail.
sections.eli5: A message can get scrambled in the mail. A short fingerprint of the message lets the reader check it is still the same.

sections.title: Generating the Field
sections.content:
Only an originating user agent generates the field. Relays and gateways are expressly forbidden to. Its use is optional but recommended when data integrity is wanted and Privacy-Enhanced Mail is not available. It may be added only to leaf entities, that is, any content type other than multipart or message/rfc822.

The MD5 algorithm is computed on the canonical form of the entity, before any content-transfer-encoding, with newlines as CR-LF pairs. The 128 bit digest gives 16 octets, which are base64-encoded to form the field value. Because trailing white space changes the digest, quoted-printable or base64 should be used as the content-transfer-encoding.
sections.eli5: The sender's mail program makes the fingerprint from the message in its plain, standard form. Mail relays along the way are not allowed to add one.

sections.title: Checking the Field
sections.content:
If the field is present, a recipient user agent may choose to use it to verify that the entity was not modified during transport. The receiver computes the digest on the canonical form after undoing any content-transfer-encoding.

Relays and gateways are expressly forbidden to change their processing because the field is present. A gateway may remove the field if it translates the entity into a different content-type.
sections.eli5: The reader's mail program can redo the fingerprint and compare. The post offices in the middle must not treat the package differently because of it.

sections.title: Security Limits
sections.content: The field provides a data integrity service that protects against accidental modification in transit. The RFC says only a secure integrity service, such as that of Privacy Enhanced Mail, is conjectured to protect against all modifications. So Content-MD5 should not be treated as protection against a deliberate attacker.
sections.eli5: The fingerprint catches accidents, like a bent corner. It does not stop someone who wants to swap the contents on purpose.
